The ordered identity \(A^2-B^2=AC+CB\) gives quadratic form \(\lambda v^*(A+B)v\). Again positivity forces \(\lambda >0\), proving \(C\) positive. In the nonstrict anticommutator variant, a negative \(B\) direction can sit in \(\ker A\): \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) and \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) are a counterexample. These proofs use one matrix’s eigenvectors and do not assume simultaneous diagonalization.
lessons.method: Test the target matrix’s eigenvectors and reduce the desired sign to a scalar.
lessons.pitfall: Positive matrices need not commute, and difference-of-squares factorizations cannot be reordered.

lessons.title: Rank-one commutators and a common eigenvector
lessons.statement: Over \(\mathbb C\), if \(AB-BA\) has rank one, \(A\) and \(B\) have a common eigenvector.
lessons.proof: Write \(C=uv^T\). Induct on word length \(m\) to show \(v^Twu=0\) for every word in \(A\),\(B\). At length zero this is \(\operatorname{tr}C=0\). Swapping adjacent \(AB\) and \(BA\) in a word of length \(m\) changes its value by \((v^Tw_1u)(v^Tw_2u)=0\), using shorter words. Thus words with \(i\) copies of \(A\) and \(j\) copies of \(B\) have one common value \(\alpha\). Expand \([A^{i+1},B^{j+1}]=\sum_{r=0}^i\sum_{s=0}^j A^rB^sCB^{j-s}A^{i-r}\). Cyclic trace makes every term \(\alpha\), while a commutator has trace zero. Hence \((i+1)(j+1)\alpha=0\), proving the induction in characteristic zero. Now the nonzero span \(W\) of all \(wu\) is invariant under \(A\),\(B\) and lies in ker(\(v^T\)). Their commutator vanishes on \(W\). An eigenspace of \(A\) on \(W\) is invariant under \(B\), and \(B\) has an eigenvector there over \(\mathbb C\). This is the required common vector.
lessons.method: Build an invariant subspace where the commutator vanishes before using the commuting argument.
lessons.pitfall: The rank-one commutator itself generally does not vanish on the whole space.

lessons.title: Baire category theorem
lessons.statement: A nonempty complete metric space cannot be a countable union of closed sets with empty interior. Equivalently, a countable intersection of open dense sets is dense.
lessons.proof: Let \(U\) be any nonempty open set and \(G_n\) open dense. Choose a closed ball of positive radius at most \(1/2\) inside \(U\) intersect \(G_1\). Inductively choose a closed ball of positive radius at most \(2^{-n}\) inside the preceding open ball intersect \(G_n\). Density makes that intersection nonempty, and openness supplies the smaller ball. The centers form a Cauchy sequence, since all later centers lie in each earlier ball and its diameter tends to zero. Completeness gives a limit lying in every closed ball, hence in \(U\) and every \(G_n\). If a chosen point is isolated, its singleton is open and density puts it in every \(G_n\), giving the conclusion immediately. Taking complements proves the closed-set formulation.
lessons.method: When a complete space is covered by countably many closed constraints, at least one constraint holds throughout a nonempty open set.
lessons.pitfall: Completeness is essential; the rationals are a countable union of closed singletons with empty interior.

lessons.title: Chain rule and equality of mixed partials
lessons.statement: If \(f\) is differentiable at a and \(g\) at \(f(a)\), then \(D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))Df(a)\). A \(C^2\) scalar function has equal mixed second partials.
lessons.proof: Write \(f(a+h)=f(a)+Ah+r(h)\) with \(r(h)=o(\|h\|)\). Then \(k=Ah+r(h)=O(\|h\|)\). Substituting \(g(f(a)+k)=g(f(a))+Bk+s(k)\), where \(s(k)=o(\|k\|)\), yields the derivative \(BA\) and remainder \(Br(h)+s(k)=o(\|h\|)\). For mixed partials take the rectangular difference \(f(x+h,y+k)-f(x+h,y)-f(x,y+k)+f(x,y)\). Two applications of the fundamental theorem express it as the double integral of \(f_{xy}\), and in the opposite order as that of \(f_{yx}\). Divide by \(hk\) and let both nonzero increments tend to zero. Continuity of the two second partials makes the averages tend to their values at the point, proving equality.
lessons.method: Compose linear derivatives in the order the maps act. Restrict to a rectangle within the open domain before using the integral argument.
lessons.pitfall: Existence of the partial derivatives alone does not imply differentiability or equality of mixed partials.

lessons.title: Hadamard’s determinant inequality
lessons.statement: For a square matrix with columns \(v_i\), \(|\det A|\) is at most the product of their Euclidean lengths. For nonzero columns, equality holds exactly when they are mutually orthogonal.
lessons.proof: If the columns are dependent, the determinant is zero, and equality can hold only if one column is zero. Otherwise apply Gram–Schmidt to get \(A=QR\) with \(Q\) unitary and \(R\) upper triangular. The diagonal entries are the lengths of the successive orthogonal residuals. Each is at most the corresponding column length, with equality exactly when that column was already orthogonal to all earlier columns. Since \(|\det Q|=1\), multiplying the diagonal entries proves the bound and equality criterion. The dependent case with all columns nonzero has strict inequality.
lessons.method: Apply the column version to \(A\) or the row version to its transpose; track equality separately.
lessons.pitfall: Zero columns make both sides zero without forcing all other columns to be orthogonal.

lessons.title: Cesàro averages and the Cauchy condensation test
lessons.statement: If \(a_n\to a\), then \(N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^Na_n\to a\). If \(a_n\ge0\) decreases, \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n<\infty\) iff \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty2^ka_{2^k}<\infty\).
lessons.proof: For the averages, split at \(N\) where \(|a_n-a|<\varepsilon\). The contribution of the first \(N\) terms divided by the averaging length tends to zero, and the remaining contribution has modulus at most \(\varepsilon\). For condensation, in the block \(2^k\le n<2^{k+1}\), monotonicity gives \(2^k a_{2^{k+1}}\le\sum_{n=2^k}^{2^{k+1}-1}a_n\le 2^k a_{2^k}\). Summing over blocks bounds the original series between one half of a shifted condensed series and the condensed series. Nonnegative partial sums are bounded exactly when they converge, giving the equivalence.
lessons.method: Split into a fixed initial segment and a uniformly controlled tail. For slowly decaying positive terms, group dyadic blocks.
lessons.pitfall: Convergence of arithmetic averages does not imply convergence of the original sequence.

lessons.title: Cauchy mean value theorem and \(L\)’Hôpital’s rule
lessons.statement: For real continuous \(f,g\) on \([a,b]\), differentiable inside, some \(c\in(a,b)\) satisfies \((f(b)-f(a))g\prime(c)=(g(b)-g(a))f\prime(c)\). If \(f,g\to0\) at an endpoint, \(g\prime\ne0\) nearby and \(f\prime/g\prime\to L\), then \(f/g\to L\), allowing extended real limits.
lessons.proof: Apply Rolle to \(h(t)=(f(b)-f(a))(g(t)-g(a))-(g(b)-g(a))(f(t)-f(a))\), which vanishes at both endpoints. Its zero derivative gives the identity. In the zero-over-zero case, extend both functions continuously to zero at the endpoint. The ordinary mean value theorem makes \(g\) nonzero at every nearby interior point, since \(g'\) has no zeros. Cauchy’s identity expresses \(f(x)/g(x)\) as \(f'(c)/g'(c)\) at a point between \(x\) and the endpoint. As \(x\) approaches that endpoint, so does \(c\), proving the limit. For an endpoint at infinity, substitute \(t=1/x\) to reduce to a finite endpoint; the derivative ratio is unchanged. The infinity-over-infinity variant can be proved by applying the same identity between a fixed sufficiently late point and \(x\): the increment ratio is close to \(L\) and the fixed endpoint contributions vanish relative to \(g(x)\). For infinite \(L\), use arbitrary one-sided bounds instead of an absolute-error estimate.
lessons.method: Check the indeterminate form and the derivative-ratio limit before applying the rule.
lessons.pitfall: A limit of derivative ratios alone says nothing without endpoint and denominator hypotheses.

lessons.title: Polynomial interpolation and Vandermonde matrices
lessons.statement: At \(n\ge1\) distinct scalar nodes \(t_i\), there is exactly one polynomial of degree below \(n\) with prescribed values. The evaluation matrix in the monomial basis is invertible, with determinant \(\prod_{i<j}(t_j-t_i)\).
lessons.proof: The polynomials \(L_i(t)=\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{t-t_j}{t_i-t_j}\) satisfy \(L_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}\), so their value-weighted sum gives existence. A difference of two interpolants would have \(n\) distinct roots but degree below \(n\), hence vanish. The root bound follows by successively factoring (\(t-t_i\)) using polynomial division. Thus evaluation is an isomorphism and its monomial matrix is invertible. Its determinant is the Vandermonde product: as a polynomial in the last node it has roots at all previous nodes and leading coefficient the smaller Vandermonde determinant; induction gives \(\prod_{i<j}(t_j-t_i)\).
lessons.method: Use the evaluation basis to turn conditions at distinct points into coordinates.
lessons.pitfall: Repeated nodes need derivative conditions and Hermite interpolation instead.

lessons.title: Idempotents and invariant direct sums
lessons.statement: If \(P^2=P\), then \(V=\operatorname{ran}P\oplus\ker P\), and \(P\) is identity on its range and zero on its kernel. Commuting operators preserve one another’s kernels and eigenspaces.
lessons.proof: Write \(v=Pv+(v-Pv)\). The first summand lies in the range and the second in the kernel. If \(w\) is in both, write \(w=Pu\) and note \(Pw=P^2u=Pu=w\), while \(Pw=0\); hence \(w=0\). In a basis of the two summands \(P\) is \(\operatorname{diag}(I,0)\), so its rank equals its trace in characteristic zero. Conversely a chosen direct sum defines such a projection. If \(ST=TS\) and \(Tv=\lambda  v\), then \(T(Sv)=S(Tv)=\lambda Sv\). The same calculation with polynomials of \(T\) proves invariance of generalized eigenspaces. Commuting diagonalizable complex operators are simultaneously diagonalizable: decompose into eigenspaces of one, restrict the others, and repeat; each restriction stays diagonalizable because its square-free annihilating polynomial still annihilates it.
lessons.method: Construct the direct sum explicitly before asserting similarity to a block projection.
lessons.pitfall: An idempotent need not be an orthogonal projection; self-adjointness is also required.

lessons.title: Induced norms and polarization
lessons.statement: An induced operator norm satisfies \(\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|\) and \(|\|A\|-\|B\||\le\|A-B\|\). A linear map preserving inner-product norms preserves inner products.
lessons.proof:
For each unit vector, \(\|ABx\|\le\|A\|\|Bx\|\le\|A\|\|B\|\). Taking the supremum proves submultiplicativity. The triangle inequality gives \(\|A\|\le\|A-B\|+\|B\|\); swap \(A\),\(B\) for the reverse bound. In the linear-first convention, expand squared norms to obtain
\[\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle=\frac{\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2}{4},\qquad\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle=\frac{\|x+iy\|^2-\|x-iy\|^2}{4}.\]
Norm preservation and linearity preserve these expressions, hence the full inner product. A square finite-dimensional isometry is injective and therefore onto, so unitary. SVD gives \(\|Ax\|^2=\sum_i s_i^2|c_i|^2\) in singular coordinates; taking the maximum over unit vectors proves \(\|A\|_2=\max_i s_i\).
lessons.method: Test unit vectors and use SVD for sharp norm bounds. Keep the convention straight in polarization.
lessons.pitfall: An isometry in infinite dimension need not be onto.

lessons.title: Polynomial spectral mapping
lessons.statement: For a complex square matrix and polynomial \(p\), \(\sigma(p(A))=p(\sigma(A))\). Algebraic multiplicities of eigenvalues with equal images add; eigenspaces can grow.
lessons.proof: Triangularize \(A\) over the complex numbers. Polynomial operations preserve upper triangular form and put \(p(\lambda_i)\) on its diagonal. The characteristic polynomial of \(p(A)\) is therefore the product of \(t-p(\lambda_i)\), proving the spectrum and multiplicity statement. Independently, any eigenvector of \(A\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is an eigenvector of \(p(A)\) with value \(p(\lambda )\). But this implication alone does not give the converse for individual eigenvectors. If a polynomial has simple roots and annihilates \(A\), the generalized-eigenspace decomposition shows diagonalizability; repeated roots allow nontrivial Jordan blocks.
lessons.method: For matrix polynomials, use triangular form to get the full spectrum, then study Jordan blocks for finer information.
lessons.pitfall: Distinct eigenvalues of \(A\) can have the same polynomial image.

lessons.title: Fourier orthogonality and Parseval
lessons.statement: For any bounded Riemann-integrable complex function on \([-\pi,\pi]\), let \(c_k=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^\pi f(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx\). Then \(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|c_k|^2=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^\pi|f|^2\). The periodic extension may jump at its endpoints.
lessons.proof: Use the normalized integral inner product. The exponentials \(e^{ikx}\) are orthonormal by direct integration. Orthogonal projection onto their finite span gives the Pythagorean identity \(\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{|k|\le N}|c_k|^2+\|f-S_N\|_2^2\). Real trigonometric polynomials form an algebra on the circle, contain constants, and separate points because the pair \((\cos x,\sin x)\) identifies a circle point. Stone–Weierstrass makes them uniformly dense in real continuous periodic functions; taking real and imaginary parts gives complex density. Given \(\varepsilon\) choose a trigonometric polynomial \(p\) with \(\|f-p\|_2<\varepsilon\). For \(N\) covering its frequencies, the closest-point property of the projection gives \(\|f-S_N\|_2\le\|f-p\|_2<\varepsilon\). Thus the remainder norm tends to zero and the Pythagorean identity yields Parseval. This proves convergence in the integral squared norm, without claiming pointwise or uniform convergence of the Fourier partial sums. For bounded Riemann-integrable \(f\), first approximate it in the integral squared norm by step functions: the Darboux criterion gives a lower step approximation with arbitrarily small integral absolute error, and boundedness turns this into small squared error. Apply this separately to real and imaginary parts. Replace each of the finitely many step jumps by linear ramps in intervals of arbitrarily small total length; also join the endpoint values to obtain a continuous periodic function. The modifications stay bounded and have arbitrarily small squared integral error. Thus continuous periodic functions, and consequently trigonometric polynomials, are dense for each such \(f\). The same projection argument proves Parseval for this larger class, including a noninteger exponential restricted to the interval.
lessons.method: Compute coefficients with integration by parts, then use Parseval to convert an integral norm into a numerical series.
lessons.pitfall: Parseval does not imply uniform convergence of the Fourier series.

lessons.title: Darboux’s theorem for derivatives
lessons.statement: If \(f\) is differentiable on an interval, its derivative has the intermediate value property: between any two derivative values it assumes every intermediate value. Continuity of the derivative is unnecessary.
lessons.proof: Let \(a<b\) and let \(\lambda\) lie strictly between \(f'(a)\) and \(f'(b)\). Define \(h(x)=f(x)-\lambda x\) on \([a,b]\). If \(h'(a)<0<h'(b)\), small inward increments at each endpoint lower the value, so neither endpoint minimizes \(h\). Continuity and compactness give an interior minimum \(c\), where \(h'(c)=0\) by Fermat. Thus \(f'(c)=\lambda\). If the signs are reversed, use an interior maximum. Endpoint derivative values in the statement may be interpreted as derivatives at interior points of the original domain; the interval between them is a compact subinterval. This proves every intermediate value occurs without imposing continuous derivatives. More generally a function with the Darboux property maps every interval to an interval, by the definition of that property.
lessons.method: When derivative continuity is unavailable, extremize \(f(x)-\lambda x\) instead of applying the ordinary intermediate value theorem to \(f'\).
lessons.pitfall: The intermediate value property does not imply continuity: derivatives can be discontinuous.

definitions.question: What is the Darboux property?
definitions.answer: Whenever \(a<b\) and \(\lambda\) lies between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\), some \(c\) in \([a,b]\) has \(f(c)=\lambda\).
